title: Drones: design and control
description: Build and size a multirotor: motors, propellers, battery and flight time; then tune the PID control of altitude and attitude, plan a GPS mission and learn the ANAC and DECEA rules (Brazil).

drone-01-partes.title: The parts of a drone
drone-01-partes.theory:
# Anatomy of a multirotor

A multirotor drone (quadcopter, hexacopter…) has no control surfaces: it is controlled **only by varying the speed of each motor**.

- **Frame (chassis)**: the arms and the central plate, usually carbon fibre. The size is the distance between opposite motors (e.g. 250 mm).
- **Brushless motors**: no brushes, very efficient. The **KV** constant says how many rpm per volt the motor spins with no load: a 2300 KV motor at 11.1 V spins ~25,500 rpm.
- **ESC** (electronic speed controller): one per motor; turns the flight controller's command into three-phase current for the motor.
- **Propellers**: half spin clockwise (CW) and half counter-clockwise (CCW), to cancel the torque. The notation 5x4.3 means 5 inches in diameter and 4.3 of pitch.
- **LiPo battery**: cells of 3.7 V nominal (4.2 V full). "3S" = 3 cells in series = 11.1 V. Capacity is given in mAh.
- **Flight controller (FC)**: a microcontroller with an **IMU** (gyroscope + accelerometer) that runs the PID control hundreds to thousands of times per second.
- **Radio receiver**, **GPS**, **camera** and **telemetry**, depending on the application.

## How it moves

- **Up/down**: all the motors speed up or slow down together.
- **Tilt (roll/pitch)**: motors on one side spin more than those on the other.
- **Turn (yaw)**: speed up the motors spinning in one direction and slow down those in the other — the reaction torque turns the drone.
drone-01-partes.safety: Drone propellers cut: always remove the propellers when working on the electronics or configuring the drone on the bench. LiPo batteries can catch fire if punctured, crushed or charged incorrectly.

questions.prompt: A **2300 KV** motor is connected to an **11.1 V** battery. How many rpm does it spin with no load?
questions.explanation: rpm = KV × V = 2300 × 11.1 = 25,530 rpm (with a propeller, it spins less).

questions.prompt: Why do half the propellers spin clockwise and half counter-clockwise?
options: So the motors' reaction torques cancel and the drone does not spin by itself
Because motors only spin one way
questions.explanation: Each motor turns the drone the opposite way; with half in each direction, the torques cancel. By unbalancing on purpose, the drone yaws.

questions.prompt: Which part turns the flight controller's command into current for the brushless motor?
questions.explanation: The ESC (Electronic Speed Controller) switches the three-phase current that makes the brushless motor spin.

questions.prompt: A **4S** battery has a nominal voltage of how many volts?
questions.explanation: 4 cells × 3.7 V = 14.8 V (16.8 V full).

questions.prompt: How does a quadcopter **yaw** (turn on its own axis)?
options: Speeding up the motors spinning in one direction and slowing down those in the other
questions.explanation: The total thrust stays the same (it neither rises nor falls), but the reaction torque becomes unbalanced and the drone turns.

drone-02-empuxo-peso.title: Thrust and weight
drone-02-empuxo-peso.theory:
# The most important calculation of the drone

To leave the ground, the total thrust of the motors must be greater than the weight. The ratio between the two is the **thrust-to-weight (T/W)**:

```
T/W = (number of motors × max thrust per motor) / total mass
```

In practice, manufacturers give thrust in **grams** (gf). Example: 4 motors of 800 g on a 1600 g drone → T/W = 2.

## How much is enough?

- **T/W < 1**: does not take off.
- **T/W ≈ 1.5**: takes off, but with no margin for wind or manoeuvres — dangerous.
- **T/W ≈ 2**: the recommended minimum for filming and cargo drones.
- **T/W 5–10**: racing and acrobatic drones.

## Hover throttle

If the thrust is proportional to the throttle (the approximation used here), the drone hovers at:

```
hover throttle ≈ 1 / (T/W)
```

T/W = 2 → hovers at **50%** throttle, leaving 50% to climb, brake and correct.

This drone has a **150 g** camera installed. The battery mass also counts (the simulator calculates it: LiPo ≈ 150 Wh/kg).
drone-02-empuxo-peso.task: With the 150 g camera installed, make the drone have **T/W ≥ 2** and hover at **50% throttle at most**.
drone-02-empuxo-peso.safety: Always test motors and propellers fixed to a bench, away from your face and hands, and with the battery disconnected while assembling.
hints: Stronger motors increase thrust; a lighter frame reduces weight.
Motors with 450 g of thrust each solve it.

questions.prompt: A **1600 g** drone has **4 motors of 800 g** maximum thrust. What is the T/W?
With T/W = 2, at what % of throttle does it hover (thrust proportional to throttle)?
Why is it not enough to have a T/W just above 1?
options: Because the drone gets too fast
Because there is no thrust left to climb, brake, correct wind gusts and compensate for the battery discharging
Because the camera does not work
questions.explanation: The controller needs margin: to tilt, one side speeds up; to brake a descent, all of them speed up. Without margin, the drone loses control.

drone-03-bateria.title: Battery and flight time
drone-03-bateria.theory:
# Energy in the battery

A battery's energy is voltage × charge:

```
Energy (Wh) = Voltage (V) × Capacity (Ah)
```

A 4S 2200 mAh: 14.8 V × 2.2 Ah = **32.6 Wh**.

## How long does it fly?

```
time (h) = usable capacity (Ah) / current (A)
```

Only ~**80%** of the capacity is used (discharging to the end ruins the LiPo). The hover current comes from the power: `I = P / V`.

In the simulator, the hover power comes from momentum theory per propeller (`P = T^1.5/√(2ρA)`), with a figure of merit of 0.55 and motor+ESC efficiency of 75%.

## The battery dilemma

Bigger battery = more energy, but also **more weight**, which requires **more power**. Beyond a certain point, increasing the battery hardly increases the flight time (see the time × capacity graph). That is why long-endurance drones use batteries with more Wh/kg (Li-ion) or bigger, more efficient motors and propellers.

- More **cells** (higher voltage) for the same capacity = more energy, with lower current (less loss in the wires).
drone-03-bateria.task: Make this drone fly for at least **10 minutes**, keeping **T/W ≥ 2**.
drone-03-bateria.safety: **LiPo batteries** can catch fire violently. Always charge under supervision, with a balance charger, inside a fire-resistant bag and away from flammable materials. Never discharge below ~3.3 V per cell, never use swollen or punctured batteries, and store them at ~3.8 V per cell.
hints: More cells and more mAh increase the energy — and the weight. You may need stronger motors to keep T/W.
4S with 2600 mAh and 600 g motors fly 11 minutes.

questions.prompt: How much energy does a **4S 2200 mAh** battery have?
Using 80% of a **2200 mAh** battery, how many minutes does the drone fly drawing **15 A**?
Why does doubling the battery capacity **not** double the flight time?
options: Because the bigger battery has less energy
Because the bigger battery weighs more, and the drone needs more power to support that weight
Because the motors do not accept more current
questions.explanation: Hover power grows with the weight raised to 1.5; part of the extra energy is spent just carrying the battery itself.

drone-04-helice.title: Choosing the propeller
drone-04-helice.theory:
# Big propeller, slow motor

For the same thrust, a **bigger** propeller pushes **more air more slowly**, and that costs less energy (the same idea as the helicopter rotor):

```
P_ideal = T^1.5 / √(2 · ρ · A)        A = π · D² / 4
```

Since A ∝ D², the ideal power falls with **1/D**: doubling the diameter halves the power.

Efficiency is usually given in **grams of thrust per watt (g/W)**: racing drones sit at 3–5 g/W; long-endurance drones with large propellers, 8–12 g/W.

## So why not always use huge propellers?

- The frame has to be bigger (the propellers cannot touch).
- Large propellers have more **inertia**: the motor takes longer to change speed, and the drone responds more slowly (worse for racing and acrobatics).
- They need **low-KV** motors with more torque.

## Notation

`10x4.5`: 10 inches in diameter, 4.5 inches of **pitch** (how far the propeller "advances" in one turn, like a screw). Higher pitch = more speed, more current.

The graph shows the flight time for each propeller size, keeping the rest of the drone.
drone-04-helice.task: Build a drone that flies **at least 15 minutes** with an efficiency of **at least 8 g/W**.
drone-04-helice.safety: Larger propellers store a lot of energy: a 10" propeller at 8000 rpm has a tip moving at over 100 km/h. Never hold a powered-on drone in your hand and use propeller guards around people.
hints: Increase the propeller and watch the flight time rise on the graph. Large propellers need motors with more thrust.
9" propeller, 800 g motors and a 4S 2200 mAh battery.

questions.prompt: Keeping the thrust, if the propeller diameter **doubles**, the ideal power is multiplied by how much?
questions.explanation: The area becomes 4× larger; P ∝ 1/√A = 1/√4 = 0.5. The power halves.

questions.prompt: What does the **5x4.3** propeller mean?
options: 5 inches in diameter and 4.3 inches of pitch
questions.explanation: First number = diameter, second = pitch, both in inches.

questions.prompt: Why do racing drones use **small** propellers?
options: Because they have little inertia and change speed very quickly, giving agile responses
questions.explanation: Agility comes from the fast response of the motors; efficiency takes a back seat.

drone-05-imu-sensores.title: IMU and sensors
drone-05-imu-sensores.theory:
# How does the drone know where it is?

The flight controller needs to know, hundreds of times per second, the drone's **tilt**, **height** and **direction**.

## The IMU (inertial measurement unit)

- **Gyroscope**: measures **angular velocity** (°/s) on 3 axes. Integrating over time gives the angle, but small errors accumulate: the angle **drifts**.
- **Accelerometer**: measures acceleration, including **gravity**. At rest, it points "down" and gives the tilt angle — but motor **vibration** and flight accelerations make it noisy.
- **Magnetometer** (compass): gives the direction (yaw) from the Earth's magnetic field; it suffers interference from high-current cables.
- **Barometer**: measures air pressure → altitude (resolution of ~10 cm, but it varies with wind and weather).
- **GPS**: absolute position and speed (we will see it later).

## Sensor fusion: the complementary filter

The gyroscope is good in the short term; the accelerometer, in the long term. The **complementary filter** combines the two:

```
angle = 0.98 · (angle + gyro · dt) + 0.02 · accelerometer_angle
```

Modern controllers use the **Kalman filter** (or its variants, like ArduPilot's EKF), which weights each sensor by its uncertainty.

questions.prompt: What does the **gyroscope** measure?
questions.explanation: The MEMS gyroscope measures how fast the drone rotates on each axis (°/s or rad/s).

questions.prompt: Why not use only the accelerometer to know the tilt?
options: Because it does not measure gravity
Because vibrations and flight accelerations mix with gravity and make the measurement noisy
Because it only works with GPS
questions.explanation: The accelerometer measures the sum of gravity and the motion accelerations; in the short term it is noisy.

questions.prompt: Complementary filter: previous angle **10°**, gyro **20 °/s**, dt = **0.01 s**, accelerometer reads **12°**. What is the new angle?
A gyroscope has an error (drift) of **0.5 °/s**. Without correction, how far off is the calculated angle after **60 s**?
questions.explanation: 0.5 °/s × 60 s = 30° — that is why it must be corrected with the accelerometer.

questions.prompt: Which sensor does the drone use to hold **height** when there is no GPS?
questions.explanation: The barometer measures atmospheric pressure, which falls about 12 Pa for every metre climbed near the ground.

drone-06-pid-altura.title: PID control: holding the height
drone-06-pid-altura.theory:
# Closed-loop control

The controller measures the **error** `e = target − measured` and calculates the command. The **PID** controller adds three terms:

```
output = Kp·e + Ki·∫e·dt + Kd·de/dt
```

- **P (proportional)**: corrects in proportion to the error. On its own, it leaves a **steady-state error** when there is a constant load (here, gravity): to hover at 50% throttle with Kp = 10 %/m, an error of 50/10 = **5 m** remains. Too high a Kp makes the drone **oscillate**.
- **I (integral)**: adds up the error over time and keeps raising the command until the error disappears — it **eliminates the steady-state error**. Too much I causes overshoot and slow oscillation.
- **D (derivative)**: reacts to the **speed** at which the error changes — it is a **brake** that damps the approach to the target. Here it is applied to the climb speed ("derivative on measurement"), so there is no jolt when the target changes.

## How to measure quality

- **Overshoot**: how far it went past the target (% of the target).
- **Settling time**: when it enters and stays within ±5% of the target.
- **Steady-state error**: what remains at the end.

## Practical tuning recipe

1. Start with I = D = 0 and increase **P** until it responds quickly (an error will remain and it will oscillate).
2. Increase **D** until the oscillations disappear.
3. Increase **I** slowly until the final error is zero.

The simulator includes the motor response (~30 ms delay) and the integrator "freezes" when the throttle saturates (anti-windup).
drone-06-pid-altura.task: Tune the PID to take the drone to **10 m** with **overshoot ≤ 10%**, **settling within 6 s** and **no error at the end**.
hints: With P alone it does not reach the target: the final error is (hover throttle)/Kp. Use I to zero the error and D to damp.
Kp = 12, Ki = 4 and Kd = 10 work well.
goals: Reaches and stays at the target height (±5%)

questions.prompt: With **P** control only, the drone hovers at **50%** throttle and Kp = **10 %/m**. What height error remains?
questions.explanation: To give 50% throttle, Kp·e = 50 → e = 50/10 = 5 m below the target.

questions.prompt: Which PID term eliminates the steady-state error?
questions.explanation: The integral accumulates the error and keeps growing until it is zero.

questions.prompt: The drone overshoots the target and oscillates. Which term should you increase first?
questions.explanation: The derivative acts against the approach speed, damping the oscillation.

drone-07-atitude.title: Attitude vs altitude: the roll PID
drone-07-atitude.theory:
# The inner loop

To go forward, the drone **tilts** (attitude) and part of the thrust becomes horizontal force. That is why control is done in **cascade**:

```
position → (outer PID) → desired angle → (attitude PID) → thrust difference → (motors)
```

- The **attitude** loop (inner) must be much **faster** than the position/altitude loop (outer): it runs at 1–8 kHz in modern controllers.
- Many controllers also use an **angular rate** loop inside the angle loop.

## The physics of roll

To roll, the motors on one side speed up and those on the other slow down. The torque is the thrust difference × arm, and the angular acceleration is torque / moment of inertia. Small drones are extremely agile (thousands of °/s²).

## Why D is indispensable here

There is almost no natural damping in roll, and the motors take a few milliseconds to change speed. With **P** alone the drone **oscillates** more and more. **D** brakes the rotation; **I** compensates constant disturbances — here, a side wind / shifted CG that asks for 5% of the maximum torque all the time.

The gains are in % of thrust difference per degree of error (Kp), per degree·second (Ki) and per °/s (Kd).
drone-07-atitude.task: Tune the roll PID to tilt **20°** with **overshoot ≤ 10%**, **settling within 0.5 s** and final error within ±5%.
hints: First add D until the oscillation disappears; then I to beat the constant wind.
Kp = 1.5, Ki = 2 and Kd = 0.2.
goals: Reaches and stays at the target angle (±5%)

questions.prompt: In a cascade control (position → attitude → motors), which loop must be the fastest?
questions.explanation: The inner loop must respond much faster than the outer one so that the outer one "sees" the inner one as almost instantaneous.

questions.prompt: A control loop runs at **1 kHz**. What is the interval between two calculations, in milliseconds?
Why does the drone oscillate in roll with P alone?
options: Because there is almost no natural damping and the motor delay makes the correction arrive late; the D term is missing
questions.explanation: Without a term that reacts to angular velocity, the drone overshoots the target, corrects late again and the oscillation grows.

drone-08-gps-navegacao.title: GPS and navigation: round trip
drone-08-gps-navegacao.theory:
# How GPS works

GNSS satellites (American GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou) transmit the exact time. The receiver measures **how long the signal took** from each satellite and calculates the distance. With **4 satellites** it solves 4 unknowns: x, y, z and its own clock error.

- Typical accuracy: **2–5 m** horizontally (worse vertically).
- **RTK**: a fixed base sends corrections and the accuracy reaches **centimetres** (mapping, precision agriculture).

## Waypoint missions

The autopilot (ArduPilot, PX4) follows a list of **waypoints** (latitude, longitude, altitude) and, at the end, does the **RTH** (return to home).

## Energy in forward flight

Flying forward, the drone tilts and the rotor meets "fresh" air (translational lift): the induced power **drops**. But the body drag grows with v². There is a **best-range speed** (minimum Wh per km) — see the graph.

```
Mission energy = Σ power × time   (climb, outbound, return, descent)
```

The safety rule here: use at most **80%** of the battery (20% reserve) and have **T/W ≥ 1.5** to cope with wind.
drone-08-gps-navegacao.task: Plan an inspection at a point **3 km** from the base (round trip): the mission must be **completed with a 20% reserve** and use **at most 75% of the battery**.
drone-08-gps-navegacao.safety: Always plan a battery reserve (here, 20%) and a safe return point. Loss of GPS or radio signal happens: set the automatic return mode (RTH) and a return height above trees and buildings.
hints: Too slow, and the drone spends too much time in the air; see the lowest Wh/km speed on the graph.
12 m/s with a 2200 mAh battery solves it.
goals: Uses at most 75% of the battery

questions.prompt: What is the minimum number of satellites a GPS receiver needs to calculate a 3D position?
questions.explanation: There are 4 unknowns: x, y, z and the receiver's clock error.

questions.prompt: Flying at **12 m/s** for **5 min**, what distance does the drone cover, in km?
To map a field with centimetre accuracy, which technology should you use?
questions.explanation: RTK uses corrections from a base station and reaches 1–2 cm.

drone-09-regras.title: Rules and safety: ANAC, DECEA and ANATEL (Brazil)
drone-09-regras.theory:
# Who regulates drones in Brazil

> This lesson uses the **Brazilian** rules as the example. In your country, check the local aviation authority (for example the FAA in the USA, EASA in Europe) and the radio regulator before flying.

- **ANAC** (National Civil Aviation Agency): rules for the aircraft and the pilot — **RBAC-E no. 94**.
- **DECEA** (Airspace Control Department, of the Air Force): use of the **airspace** — ICA 100-40 and the **SARPAS** system, where flight authorisation is requested.
- **ANATEL**: type approval of the drone's and the controller's **radios**.

## Main points (summary for study)

- Drones over **250 g** must be **registered** with ANAC (**SISANT** system); those up to 250 g have simpler rules.
- The reference height for common operations is up to **120 m (400 ft)** above ground.
- Do not fly within **30 m** (horizontally) of people who have not agreed to the operation (except for the cases provided, such as drones up to 250 g).
- Keep the drone in **visual line of sight (VLOS)**, unless in specially authorised operations.
- Stay away from **airports, heliports** and restricted areas; request airspace access through **SARPAS** when required.
- **Non-recreational** use above 250 g requires civil liability **insurance** (RETA).
- Respect **privacy**: filming people and other people's property has legal implications.

## Safety in practice

- Checklist before every flight: propellers, battery, GPS with enough satellites, return point recorded, wind.
- Never fly over crowds or near power lines.
drone-09-regras.safety: The rules change: before flying, check the current versions of RBAC-E no. 94 (ANAC), ICA 100-40 (DECEA) and ANATEL's guidance — or the equivalent rules of your own country. Flying without authorisation can lead to fines and even criminal prosecution if it puts people at risk.

questions.prompt: Which body is responsible for the **airspace** and the SARPAS system?
questions.explanation: DECEA, part of the Air Force Command, controls Brazilian airspace.

questions.prompt: From how many grams does a drone need to be registered with ANAC (SISANT)?
questions.explanation: Drones with a maximum take-off weight above 250 g need registration.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum reference height for common drone operations, in metres above ground?
questions.explanation: 120 m (400 ft) above ground level is the reference used by DECEA for common operations.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum horizontal distance from people who have **not** agreed to the flight?
questions.explanation: RBAC-E no. 94 requires 30 m horizontal distance from non-consenting people (with provided exceptions).

questions.prompt: What does flying in **VLOS** mean?
options: Keeping the drone always visible to the naked eye of the pilot
questions.explanation: VLOS = Visual Line Of Sight, without binoculars or only through the camera.

drone-10-projeto-entrega.title: Project: delivery drone
drone-10-projeto-entrega.theory:
# Mission sizing

Drone engineers solve a circular problem: the battery must have energy for the mission, but the battery weighs, which increases the power, which requires more battery…

## The roadmap

1. **Requirements**: payload (1 kg), distance (4 km to the point), reserve (20%), thrust margin (T/W ≥ 2 with the payload).
2. **Mass estimate**: frame + motors + electronics + battery + payload.
3. **Propulsion**: choose the number of motors, propellers and motors that give T/W ≥ 2 **with the payload**, in an efficient range (g/W).
4. **Energy**: add up hover at take-off, outbound (with payload), return (without the payload — lighter!) and landing:

```
E = P_hover·t1 + P_out·(d/v) + P_return·(d/v) + P_landing·t2
Battery needed = E / 0.8          (20% reserve)
```

5. **Cruise speed**: near the one with the lowest Wh/km.
6. **Iterate** until everything closes — and check the practical constraints (size, cost, redundancy: a hexa or octo keeps flying if it loses a motor).

## Mass fraction

In well-designed drones, the battery is **30–40%** of the total mass. Above that, the gain in endurance is small.
drone-10-projeto-entrega.task: Design the drone to deliver **1 kg over 4 km** and return: mission completed with reserve, **T/W ≥ 2 with the payload** and using **at most 60% of the battery**.
drone-10-projeto-entrega.safety: Drone deliveries over populated areas require special authorisation from ANAC and DECEA (or your country's equivalent), risk analysis and redundant equipment. This is a sizing exercise, not a real flight plan.
hints: With the payload, the current motors do not give T/W 2: more motors or stronger motors. The battery also needs to grow.
Hexacopter (6 motors) of 1400 g, 12" propellers, 6S and 8000 mAh.
goals: Delivery made and returns with a 20% reserve
Uses at most 60% of the battery

questions.prompt: A mission requires **800 W** for **10 min**. How many Wh of energy?
To keep a **20% reserve**, what is the minimum battery energy for that mission?
questions.explanation: Only 80% can be used: 133.3 / 0.8 = 166.7 Wh.

questions.prompt: Why does the return trip of a delivery use less energy than the outbound?
options: Because the wind always helps on the way back
Because the drone returns without the payload: lighter, it needs less thrust and less power
Because the battery gets lighter as it discharges
questions.explanation: Power grows with weight (P ∝ W^1.5 when hovering); without the package, the drone uses much less. (Lithium batteries do not get lighter as they discharge.)

drone-11-lipo.title: Inside the LiPo battery: current, C rating and internal resistance
drone-11-lipo.theory:
# Much more than "mAh"

In lesson 3 we saw energy (Wh) and flight time. A drone battery also has to **deliver high current** without losing voltage or overheating.

## C rating

The **C** rating says how many times its capacity the battery can deliver as continuous current:

```
max current = capacity (Ah) × C
```

A 1500 mAh 100C promises 1.5 × 100 = **150 A** (label numbers tend to be optimistic). A racing drone pulls peaks of 100 A or more; a filming drone, 15–30 A.

## Internal resistance and voltage sag

Each cell has a small internal resistance R (a few mΩ). Under current I:

```
voltage drop = I × R_total
heat loss    = I² × R_total
```

A 4S with 5 mΩ per cell (20 mΩ in total) pulling 60 A loses **1.2 V** and turns **72 W** into heat. That's why the voltage "sags" when you punch the throttle, and old batteries (higher R) get hot and lose punch.

## From power to current

```
I = P / V
```

A drone hovering at **300 W** on a 4S (14.8 V) pulls ~**20 A**. On 6S (22.2 V), the same power takes only 13.5 A — less I²R loss, thinner wires.

## Care

A LiPo is concentrated energy: a short circuit, puncture or overcharge can cause a **lithium fire**, which is hard to put out. Respect the minimum (3.3 V under load) and maximum (4.2 V) voltages per cell.
drone-11-lipo.safety:
- Charge LiPos **only with a balance charger**, on a non-flammable surface, in sight, inside a fireproof bag or box.
- A **swollen, dented or punctured** battery goes to proper disposal — never back into the drone.
- Store at **storage voltage** (~3.8 V per cell) and never discharge below ~3.3 V per cell under load.
- In a lithium fire, step away; use sand or a suitable extinguisher, and never breathe the smoke.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum continuous current of a **1500 mAh**, **100C** battery?
A **4S** battery has **5 mΩ** of internal resistance per cell. How much does the voltage drop when pulling **60 A**?
How much power turns into heat inside that battery at 60 A?
A drone hovers using **300 W** on a 4S battery (**14.8 V**). How much current does it draw?
What should you do with a LiPo that has **swollen**?
options: Puncture it to let the gas out and keep using it
Stop using it and dispose of it properly (discharged, at a collection point)
Charge it at a higher current to "deflate" it
questions.explanation: Swelling means internal decomposition and fire risk. Never puncture it: lithium reacts with air.

drone-12-bateria-ideal.title: The ideal battery size
drone-12-bateria-ideal.theory:
# More battery, more weight

Doubling the battery doubles the energy, but also increases the drone's mass — and the power to hover grows **faster than the mass**. By momentum theory:

```
P_hover ∝ m^1.5
```

A drone 30% heavier needs 1.3^1.5 ≈ **1.48 times** the power. That's why flight time grows less and less with capacity — up to a point where adding battery makes the flight **worse**.

## How much energy weighs

A LiPo holds ~150 Wh/kg. A 4S 5000 mAh stores 14.8 × 5 = 74 Wh and weighs ~**493 g**.

## The other constraint: thrust-to-weight

Even if flight time keeps rising, a heavy battery **eats the thrust margin**. Below T/W ≈ 2 the drone is slow to react, struggles in wind and lacks the force to stop a descent. The ideal battery is the one giving the longest flight time **while keeping T/W ≥ 2**.

## Rule of thumb

In well-designed multirotors the battery is usually **30–40% of the takeoff mass**. Below that you have performance to spare and little endurance; above, the drone "hangs" from its propellers.

## In this lab

An 800 g quadcopter (without battery), 4 motors of 700 g thrust, 9" props, 4S battery. The plot shows flight time versus capacity.
drone-12-bateria-ideal.task: Choose the battery **capacity** so the drone hovers for **at least 21 minutes** without letting **thrust-to-weight drop below 2**.
hints: Try 3000, 4500 and 6000 mAh and note the flight time and T/W of each.
The window is narrow: between ~5300 and ~6000 mAh.
goals: Flight time of at least 21 min

questions.prompt: How much does a **4S 5000 mAh** battery weigh at **150 Wh/kg**? (3.7 V per cell)
If the drone gets **30% heavier**, the hover power is multiplied by how much? (P ∝ m^1.5)
questions.explanation: 1.3^1.5 ≈ 1.48: almost 50% more power for 30% more mass.

questions.prompt: Why does doubling the battery capacity **not** double the flight time?
options: Because the bigger battery has a lower voltage
Because the extra battery weighs, and hover power grows faster than mass
Because only 50% of the battery can be used
questions.explanation: Energy ∝ capacity, but power ∝ m^1.5: each extra mAh buys fewer minutes.

drone-13-motor-kv.title: Choosing motor and propeller: KV, torque and pitch speed
drone-13-motor-kv.theory:
# What KV means

The **KV** of a brushless motor is how many **rpm per volt** it spins **with no load**:

```
no-load rpm = KV × V
```

A 920 KV motor on a 4S (14.8 V) spins ~**13 600 rpm** free (with a propeller, some 15–25% less).

## KV and torque are two sides of the same coin

The torque constant Kt (N·m per ampere) is the **inverse** of KV (in SI units):

```
Kt = 60 / (2π × KV) ≈ 9.55 / KV
```

**Low-KV** motor = more torque per amp → spins **big propellers** slowly, efficiently (cargo and filming drones). **High-KV** motor = spins **small propellers** very fast (racing drones). 920 KV gives Kt ≈ 0.0104 N·m/A: at 20 A, ~0.21 N·m.

## The propeller

A **10x4.5** propeller is 10" in diameter with a 4.5" **pitch** (how far it "advances" per turn, like a screw). The **pitch speed** is a theoretical limit of the speed of the air it pushes:

```
v_pitch = pitch × rpm / 60
```

A 5x4.3 at 30 000 rpm: 4.3 × 0.0254 × 500 ≈ **54.6 m/s**.

## How thrust scales

For the same propeller, thrust ∝ **rpm²** and power ∝ **rpm³**. Spinning 20% faster gives 1.2² = **1.44 times** the thrust and 1.73 times the power. For the same thrust, a **bigger, slower** prop uses less (lesson 4).

## Matching them

Pick the propeller for thrust and efficiency; then the motor with a KV so that, at the battery voltage, it spins that prop at the right rpm without exceeding the **maximum current** of the motor and ESC.

questions.prompt: How many no-load rpm does a **920 KV** motor spin on a **14.8 V** battery?
What is the torque constant Kt of that 920 KV motor? (Kt = 60 / (2π × KV))
What is the pitch speed of a **5x4.3** propeller at **30 000 rpm**? (1" = 0.0254 m)
If the same propeller spins **20% faster**, thrust is multiplied by how much? (thrust ∝ rpm²)
For a cargo drone with **15"** propellers, which motor makes more sense?
options: Low KV (e.g. 400 KV): lots of torque to spin the big prop slowly
High KV (e.g. 2600 KV): more rpm is always better
The motor with the most KV per gram
questions.explanation: A big prop needs torque and low rpm; a high-KV motor would draw too much current and overheat.

drone-14-carga-pesada.title: Carrying weight: hexa, octo and 6S
drone-14-carga-pesada.theory:
# A 2 kg cinema camera

A 1.5 kg filming quadcopter with a 5 Ah battery can't lift a **2 kg** camera well: T/W drops close to 1 and the flight time collapses. There are four levers:

## 1. More motors

With 6 (hexa) or 8 (octo) motors, total thrust grows. Bonus: with 6 or more, the drone can **lose a motor** and still land (redundancy).

## 2. Bigger propellers

More disc area = less power per newton (P ∝ T^1.5 / √A). On cargo drones, 15–30" props.

## 3. Higher voltage (6S, 12S)

The same power at a higher voltage needs **less current**: I = P / V. 600 W on 6S (22.2 V) is ~27 A; on 4S it would be 40.5 A. Less current = less I²R loss in wires, ESC and battery.

## 4. Bigger battery

With the whole mass larger, the battery can (and must) grow too — again respecting T/W ≥ 2.

## Thrust per motor

```
thrust per motor = total mass × T/W / number of motors
```

For 5.3 kg, T/W = 2 and 8 motors: 5300 × 2 / 8 = **1325 g** per motor.

## In this lab

A 1500 g drone (without battery), a **2000 g** camera. In this model, the motors' mass is already included in the frame.
drone-14-carga-pesada.task: Make the drone carry the 2 kg camera with **thrust-to-weight of at least 2**, **flight time of at least 18 min** and **current of up to 35 A** in a hover. Choose the **motors**, **thrust per motor**, **propeller**, **cells** and **capacity**.
drone-14-carga-pesada.safety:
- Heavy cargo drones are **another risk category**: above 25 kg (in Brazil) they require registration and special authorisations; even below that, a 15" propeller cuts like a saw.
- Test with the **propellers removed** while setting up, and fly with the load on a secure hook, away from people.
hints: Switch to 6S and 15" props: the current drops and the efficiency rises.
An octo with 1500 g per motor and 12 000 mAh exceeds 20 minutes with T/W ≈ 2.3.
goals: Flight time of at least 18 min

questions.prompt: A drone hovers at **600 W** on a **6S** battery (22.2 V). What is the current?
questions.explanation: 600 / 22.2 ≈ 27 A (on 4S it would be 40.5 A).

questions.prompt: A **5.3 kg** drone with **8 motors** needs T/W = 2. What is the minimum maximum thrust of each motor?
What safety advantage does a **hexa** or **octo** have over a quadcopter?
options: It can lose a motor and still control the descent
It flies without a battery for a few seconds
questions.explanation: On a quad, without one motor there's no way to balance torque and thrust; with 6 or 8, the others compensate (with less margin).

drone-15-pid-pesado.title: Tuning the altitude hold of a heavy drone
drone-15-pid-pesado.theory:
# The same gains don't suit every drone

In lesson 6 you tuned the altitude PID of a light drone with a high T/W. A cargo drone is different:

- **Lower T/W** (here, ~1.6): it hovers at ~**62%** throttle and there's little left to climb or stop a descent. The controller output **saturates** easily.
- **Bigger motors and props respond more slowly**: the lag between command and thrust grows.
- **More inertia**: it takes longer to stop.

## What happens with aggressive gains

High Kp and Ki ask for 100% throttle for a long time; the drone overshoots, the integrator winds up while saturated, and the result is a large **overshoot** and a slow oscillation.

## P only, again

Without an integrator, the drone stops where Kp × error = hover throttle:

```
error = hover throttle / Kp
```

With 62.5% and Kp = 5 %/m: **12.5 m** below the target! The I term is mandatory.

## Method

1. Kd first, for damping.
2. Moderate Kp — the heavy drone doesn't have the force for abrupt responses.
3. Small Ki: just to remove the error, without winding up.

In real life, **feed-forward** (adding the estimated hover throttle) is also used so the integrator has less work to do.

## In this lab

A 3 kg hexa + 10 Ah battery + 1 kg payload, target at **30 m**.
drone-15-pid-pesado.task: Tune the PID so the heavy drone **reaches and holds 30 m**, with an overshoot of **up to 3%** and settling within **5 s**.
hints: The light drone's gains (Kp 12, Ki 4, Kd 10) overshoot more than 3% here. Lower Kp and Ki.
Something like Kp 6, Ki 1.5 and Kd 8 works.
goals: Reaches and holds the target height

questions.prompt: With **T/W = 1.6**, at what % throttle does the drone hover (thrust proportional to throttle)?
With P only and **Kp = 5 %/m**, how many metres below the target does this drone stop?
Why do aggressive gains cause a large overshoot on a **low T/W** drone?
options: Because the barometer doesn't work with a load
Because the output saturates: there's little thrust left to brake, and the integrator winds up meanwhile
questions.explanation: With little margin, the drone accelerates flat out, gains speed and can't brake in time; a full I term makes it worse.

drone-16-fusao-sensores.title: Sensor fusion: complementary and Kalman filters
drone-16-fusao-sensores.theory:
# No sensor is good on its own

- The **gyroscope** is great in the short term, but integrated it **drifts**.
- The **accelerometer** knows where "down" is in the long run, but it's **noisy** and gets confused by accelerations and vibration.
- The **barometer** measures height with ~0.5 m of noise; **GPS** gives position with metres of error and slow updates.

**Sensor fusion** combines the best of each.

## Complementary filter

```
angle = α × (angle + gyro × dt) + (1 − α) × accel_angle
α = τ / (τ + dt)
```

τ is the time constant: below it the gyro is trusted, above it the accelerometer. With τ = 0.5 s and dt = 0.01 s: α ≈ **0.980**.

## Kalman filter (the idea)

The Kalman filter keeps an estimate **and its uncertainty** (variance P). For each measurement with variance R, it blends them using the **Kalman gain**:

```
K = P / (P + R)
new_estimate = estimate + K × (measurement − estimate)
```

If the estimate is uncertain (P = 4) and the measurement is good (R = 1): K = 0.8 — the measurement is trusted a lot. Estimate 10, measurement 12 → **11.6**. Afterwards the uncertainty shrinks; between measurements it grows with the model. The **EKF** (extended Kalman filter) is the heart of flight controllers like ArduPilot and PX4.

## Noise and averaging

Averaging N independent measurements reduces the standard deviation by **√N**: 100 samples → 10 times less noise (but more delay).

## Sampling

By the Nyquist theorem, to see a 200 Hz vibration you must sample at **more than 400 Hz**; otherwise it shows up as a false slow oscillation (*aliasing*). That's why IMUs run at 1–8 kHz and filters remove the motors' vibration.

questions.prompt: In a complementary filter with **τ = 0.5 s** and **dt = 0.01 s**, what is α = τ / (τ + dt)?
The estimate has variance **P = 4** and the measurement **R = 1**. What is the Kalman gain K = P / (P + R)?
With that K, the height estimate was **10 m** and the sensor reads **12 m**. What is the new estimate?
A barometer has **1 m** of noise (standard deviation). What is the noise of the average of **100** independent readings?
To see a **200 Hz** vibration without aliasing, the sampling must be above how many Hz?
questions.explanation: Nyquist: more than 2 × 200 = 400 Hz.

drone-17-atitude-pesado.title: Attitude of a heavy hexa: motor lag
drone-17-atitude-pesado.theory:
# Copying a small drone's gains can flip the drone

The **attitude** loop (roll and pitch) is the fastest in the flight controller. On a racing quad, the motors change speed in ~20–30 ms. On a cargo hexa with 15" props, the **motor takes much longer** to spin up the heavy propeller:

```
τ ≈ 0.03 × (D / 5")^1.5 s
```

With D = 15": τ ≈ 0.156 s — five times slower.

## Lag = instability

A control loop with a large lag gets the correction **late**: when the thrust finally arrives, the drone has already gone past, and the next correction arrives late again. With high gains this becomes a **growing oscillation** until the drone flips. It's the phase margin of control theory.

## Inertia

The moment of inertia grows with mass × arm²:

```
I ≈ 0.4 × m × arm²
```

A 4 kg hexa with 0.5 m arms has I ≈ 0.4 kg·m², many times that of a racing quad.

## How to tune

- **Kp** lower than on the small drone (the plant is slow).
- **Kd** relatively higher: it "sees" the roll rate and brakes early.
- **Ki** small, only against the constant disturbance (wind, off-centre CG).

Real controllers also use **filters** on the gyro signals and sometimes **feed-forward** from the pilot's command.

## In this lab

A 3 kg hexa with 15" props and 1 kg of payload. It starts with the gains of the quadcopter from lesson 7 — and flips.
drone-17-atitude-pesado.task: With the small drone's gains, the hexa flips. Tune Kp, Ki and Kd so it **reaches 20°** of roll with an overshoot of **up to 5%** and settles within **1 s**.
hints: Cut Ki first (to ~0.5) and Kp to ~1. Then raise Kd until the overshoot is gone.
Kp 1, Ki 0.5 and Kd 0.4 work; too high a Kd makes the response sluggish.
goals: Reaches and holds the target angle

questions.prompt: What is the time constant of a motor with a **15"** propeller, by the model τ = 0.03 × (D / 5")^1.5?
What is the moment of inertia (I ≈ 0.4 × m × arm²) of a **4 kg** hexa with **0.5 m** arms?
Why do a small quad's gains make the heavy hexa flip?
options: Because the hexa has more motors to control
Because the big motors' lag makes corrections arrive late, and high gains turn into a growing oscillation
Because the hexa's gyro is worse
questions.explanation: Lag in the loop reduces the phase margin; with high Kp and Ki, the late correction pushes the wrong way and the oscillation grows.

drone-18-velocidade-alcance.title: Maximum-range speed
drone-18-velocidade-alcance.theory:
# Slow is not economical

Intuitively, flying slowly would use less battery. On a multirotor that's false, for two reasons:

1. **Hovering is already expensive**: standing still, the drone spends all its lifting power.
2. Flying forward, the rotor receives **fresh air** all the time (like a wing): the **induced power drops** with speed (Glauert's formula). Up to ~10–15 m/s, total power **decreases**!

Above that, **body drag** (∝ v²) and the drone's tilt dominate, and power rises again.

## Energy per kilometre

What matters for range is not power, it's **energy per distance**:

```
Wh/km = power (W) / speed (m/s) × 1000 / 3600
```

At 15 m/s using 170 W: 170 × 1000 / 15 / 3600 ≈ **3.15 Wh/km**. With 59.2 Wh usable (80% of 74 Wh): ≈ **18.8 km** in total.

Flying at 4 m/s can cost 3 times more energy per km than flying at 15 m/s.

## The optimal speed

The maximum-range speed is where a straight line from the origin is **tangent** to the power-versus-speed curve — the point of fewest W per m/s. With a **headwind**, fly faster than that; with a tailwind, a little slower.

## In this lab

A 1.2 kg quadcopter, 4S 5000 mAh, 10" props, inspection point **5 km** away. The plot shows Wh/km versus speed.
drone-18-velocidade-alcance.task: At 4 m/s the drone can't go and come back. Choose the **cruise speed** that gives a **maximum range of at least 8.5 km**, completes the mission and uses **up to 50%** of the battery.
hints: Look at the Wh/km plot: it has a minimum. That's where you want to fly.
Between 14 and 17 m/s the range exceeds 8.5 km.
goals: Maximum range of at least 8.5 km
Uses up to 50% of the battery

questions.prompt: A drone flies at **15 m/s** using **170 W**. How many Wh does it use per km?
With **59.2 Wh** usable and **3.148 Wh/km**, how many km does the drone fly in total?
questions.explanation: 59.2 / 3.148 ≈ 18.8 km (round trip: ~9.4 km radius, not counting takeoff and landing).

questions.prompt: Why does flying at **4 m/s** use more energy per km than flying at 15 m/s?
options: Because drag is higher when slow
Because the power is almost the hover power, and it's spent for much longer on each km
questions.explanation: At 4 m/s each km takes 250 s at ~208 W; at 15 m/s, 67 s at ~170 W. Energy = power × time.

drone-19-teoria-rotor.title: Rotor aerodynamics: disc loading, ground effect and vortex ring
drone-19-teoria-rotor.theory:
# Momentum theory, again

Each drone propeller is a small helicopter rotor. To make thrust T, it accelerates the air to the **induced velocity** vi:

```
vi = √(T / (2 ρ A))
P_ideal = T × vi = T^1.5 / √(2 ρ A)
P_real = P_ideal / FM
```

**FM** (figure of merit) is the rotor's real aerodynamic efficiency: 0.5–0.65 for drone props, up to ~0.8 for helicopter rotors.

A 10" prop (A = 0.0507 m²) making 5 N: vi ≈ 6.3 m/s, P_ideal ≈ **31.7 W**; with FM = 0.6, ~**52.9 W**.

## Disc loading

```
disc loading = T / A   (N/m²)
```

The **lower** the disc loading, the less power per newton. 5" racing drones have high disc loading (agile, inefficient); cargo drones and helicopters, low.

## Altitude

Since P ∝ 1/√ρ, flying at 3000 m (σ ≈ 0.742) costs **16% more** power — and the props lose thrust margin.

## Ground effect

Close to the ground (less than ~1 rotor diameter), the ground "holds up" the airflow: less power for the same thrust. That's why the drone "floats" and slides on landing.

## Vortex ring state (VRS)

Descending **straight down** at a speed similar to vi, the rotor enters its own downwash: the air recirculates in a ring, thrust drops and fluctuates, and **adding throttle doesn't help** (it makes it worse). The way out is to **move sideways** out of its own flow. That's why drones (and helicopters) should descend diagonally or slowly.

questions.prompt: What is the ideal power of a **10"** (0.254 m) prop making **5 N** at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³)? (P = T^1.5 / √(2ρA))
With a figure of merit of **0.6**, what is that prop's real power?
What is that prop's disc loading (5 N over 0.0507 m²)?
At 3000 m, σ = ρ/ρ0 = **0.742**. The ideal power for the same thrust is multiplied by how much? (P ∝ 1/√ρ)
The drone descends straight down fast, starts wobbling and loses thrust even with high throttle. What should you do?
options: Push even more throttle straight up
Move the drone sideways to get out of the vortex ring
questions.explanation: In the vortex ring the rotor is in its own downwash; only by leaving it (sideways or forward) does thrust return.

drone-20-projeto-mapeamento.title: Final project: a mapping drone 6 km away
drone-20-projeto-mapeamento.theory:
# Putting it all together

A cooperative needs to map an area **6 km** from its base, with a **500 g** camera. Going, mapping and coming back requires a drone that brings together the lessons of this track:

- **Thrust-to-weight ≥ 2** (lesson 2) for wind and manoeuvres.
- A **battery** of the right size (lessons 3 and 12): more energy, without drowning the T/W.
- **Voltage** and **props** (lessons 4, 13 and 14): more cells = less current; bigger props = less power.
- **Cruise speed** (lesson 18): near the maximum-range speed.
- **Reserve**: come back with at least 40% of the battery (goal of using up to 60%).

## Energy sums

```
mission energy = power × time
```

12 km (there and back) at 15 m/s take 800 s; at 180 W, that's **40 Wh**. A 6S 6000 mAh battery stores 22.2 × 6 = **133.2 Wh** — plenty, even after takeoff, landing and the mapping itself.

## How to approach it

1. Set the cruise speed for the fewest Wh/km.
2. Choose cells and capacity for the energy.
3. Choose the prop and thrust per motor for T/W ≥ 2 with the new battery.
4. Run it, see what's missing, repeat.

## In this lab

A 1.2 kg quadcopter (without battery), a 500 g camera, a point 6 km away.
drone-20-projeto-mapeamento.task: Design the drone for the 6 km mission: **complete the mission**, use **up to 60%** of the battery, **thrust-to-weight ≥ 2** and a **maximum range of at least 10 km** (for margin).
drone-20-projeto-mapeamento.safety:
- Long, automatic missions (BVLOS — beyond visual line of sight) need **specific authorisation** from the aviation authorities (ANAC/DECEA in Brazil). In ordinary flight, keep the drone **in sight**.
- Set up **automatic return** (RTH) on low battery and on signal loss, with a height above the area's obstacles.
hints: Start with the speed (~15 m/s). Then switch to 6S and a bigger battery.
With 6S 6000 mAh, a 13" prop and 1500 g motors, every goal is met.
goals: Uses up to 60% of the battery
Maximum range of at least 10 km

questions.prompt: A **12 km** round trip at **15 m/s** using **180 W**. How much energy (in Wh) do the cruise legs use?
How much energy does a **6S 6000 mAh** battery hold? (3.7 V per cell)
Why plan the mission to use **at most 60%** of the battery?
options: Because the battery only charges to 60%
To keep a reserve against headwinds, detours, waiting to land and an ageing battery
Because the GPS turns off below 40%
Because the law forbids using more
questions.explanation: Ideal plans never happen: wind on the way back, an extra mapping pass or a worn battery eat the margin quickly.
